system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2181-11-15 19:39:00 to 2181-11-20 15:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ woman with vomiting and increased G-tube output.
History of prior SBO.

COMPARISON:  ___.

SUPINE AND UPRIGHT VIEWS OF THE ABDOMEN:  A gastric tube overlies the
abdominal midline, with the locking loop and the distal portion of the tube
overlying the L1-2 vertebral bodies on the upright view, similar to the prior
study.  A spinal stimulator is again noted in the upper thoracic spine.
Surgical clips are seen in the right upper quadrant. Curvilinear densities in
the right upper abdomen are unchanged since the ___ radiograph and may
represent suture material from prior surgery or calcification related to
sclerosing mesenteritis.

Multiple loops of bowel contain air and high-density material consistent with
retained oral contrast from prior CT, with abundant high-density material
noted in the rectum, suggesting abnormally-slow motility. There is no distal
collapsed bowel or distention of proximal bowel to indicate high-grade
obstruction. However, there are multiple air- fluid levels within large and
small bowel on the upright view. The visualized lung bases are clear. There is
no free intraperitoneal air and no definite extraluminal contrast.

IMPRESSIONS:  Air and retained oral contrast within the bowel extending to the
rectum in an indeterminate pattern. Retained dense contrast in the rectum
suggests markedly abnormal motility, and may represent impacted material,
though not causing large bowel obstruction.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with vomiting.

COMPARISON:  ___.

PA AND LATERAL VIEWS OF THE CHEST:  A right-sided central venous catheter
terminates in the SVC.  Spinal stimulator hardware is stable.  A gastrostomy
tube terminates in the abdominal midline.

Lungs are well expanded and clear without consolidation or pleural effusion.
There is no pneumothorax.  The heart size is normal.  There is no hilar or
mediastinal enlargement.  Pulmonary vascularity is normal. There is no free
intraperitoneal air.

IMPRESSIONS:  No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with numerous prior abdominal surgeries, G tube
in place for repeated SBOs and low-grade fevers, ? SBO or  acute pathology.

COMPARISON:  ___, and ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiple MDCT axial images were obtained from the base of the
lungs through the proximal thighs without intravenous contrast.  Enteric
contrast was administered.  Sagittal and coronal reformats derived.

FINDINGS:

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITHOUT INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  The visualized lungs
demonstrate bibasilar atelectasis.  There is no pleural effusion or
pneumothorax.  The heart is normal in size.  There is no pericardial effusion.
There is likely a central venous catheter with its tip at the cavoatrial
junction.  The heart is normal in size.  There is no pericardial effusion.

In the abdomen, intravenous contrast limits the evaluation of solid organs.
Within this limitation, the liver, spleen, kidneys, and pancreas appear
normal.  There is thickening of the right adrenal gland again.  There is a G
tube.  The loops of small bowel, contrast and fluid-filled and measures 5.1
cm.  Again seen is extraluminal hyperdense material (series 301, image 28)
that may represent suture material versus sclerosing mesenteritis.  Within the
central bowel loop, there is a tubular structure that does not appear to be
connected to any device.  This may be a GJ remnant.  This persists from prior
studies to ___.  There is no pneumatosis or free air.  There is
no pathologic mesenteric or retroperitoneal adenopathy.  The abdominal aorta
is normal in caliber and contour.

CT PELVIS WITHOUT CONTRAST:  The rectum, bladder, distal ureters are
unremarkable.  Post-hysterectomy changes are stable.  There is no free air,
free fluid, or pathologic lymphadenopathy.  There is moderate fecal loading
with the large bowel, distended with stool and contrast.

MUSCULOSKELETAL:  There is no suspicious osteolytic or osteoblastic lesion.
The neurostimulator is seen within the lower thoracic spine.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Small bowel dilation to 5.1 cm without definite transition point and with
contrast and stool seen within the large bowel, most consistent with an early
small-bowel obstruction or an ileus.  Could consider followup imaging in 4 -6
hr.

2.  Tubing within the small bowel appears redundant and may be a remnant of a
GJ tube.  This is stable in position over numerous scans and raises the
possibility of being tethered to the bowel by fibrosis and/or causing chronic
inflammation.

COMMENT:  These results were posted to the ED dashboard at the time of
interpretation.

NOTE ADDED IN ATTENDING REVIEW: There are relatively dilated proximal small
bowel loops, with relatively collapsed distal loops, particularly in the right
lower abdomen, new since the most recent study of ___, though a similar
pattern was seen previously. There is also abundant residual contrast material
in the rectum, presumably administered on ___, which may reflect further
slowing of already abnormal motility. Taken together these findings are highly
suggestive of early or incomplete distal small bowel obstruction, though the
precise point of transition is not identified. 

There is a retained enteric tube fragment, which appears unchanged in its
general location within the small bowel of a series of studies, ie. not
propelled by peristalsis, and therefore, possibly adherent to the bowel wall.
However, this is remote from the transition in bowel-caliber and likely
unrelated to the obstructive process.

Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

procedures.long_title: Parenteral infusion of concentrated nutritional substances

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had nausea and vomiting again, and bad belly pain. I’ve been doing that G-tube venting like before, and it helped a little, but then I started vomiting again even after venting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this before with partial bowel obstructions. Did you pass any stool or gas recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a solid bowel movement with a Fleet enema yesterday—started solid, got a bit loose—but no gas. I’m still not feeling right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from today. It shows your small bowel is dilated, and there’s contrast in the large bowel, which suggests a partial blockage or ileus, similar to what you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not completely blocked? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s partial, which means things are still moving, just slowly. We’ll manage this without surgery for now. You’ll be on nothing by mouth—NPO—for a few days, and your G-tube will be left open to gravity to help drain fluid and reduce pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate being on NPO. But I guess it’s necessary. What about pain? It’s pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV morphine every six hours, starting at 6 mg. We’ll adjust it based on your pain. But we have to be careful—too many narcotics can slow your bowels even more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ve been on MS Contin at home. Can we keep that going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued your MS Contin 30 mg twice daily. We’ll also keep your pregabalin for nerve pain. And for nausea, we’re using Phenergan since you’re allergic to Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I really can’t take Zofran—it doesn’t help anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll stick with Phenergan. Your labs show your hemoglobin is low—11.2—so we think you have iron deficiency anemia, likely from malabsorption. We’ll give you IV iron—Ferrlecit—tomorrow to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve always had trouble absorbing nutrients. What about my Coumadin? I’m on it for my arm clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your warfarin at 7.5 mg daily. Your INR is therapeutic, so we’re good there. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but maybe a little less pain. My G-tube drained over 1200 cc yesterday. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s expected with a partial obstruction. The good news is your output is a sign the tube is working. We’re seeing it trend down today—already under 1000 cc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any chance I can start drinking something soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to see your bowels start moving more normally. You’re still having some distension and tenderness. We’ll repeat the CT if things don’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Your G-tube output is now down to about 600 cc. That’s a great sign. You passed a bowel movement with Miralax yesterday—your lower pain improved after that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the lower pain is gone. The upper belly pain is still there, but less sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team suggested gentle abdominal massage to help move things along. It might help relieve the remaining blockage. Would you be okay trying that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sure, I’ll try anything. Does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shouldn’t. We’ll do it gently. The idea is to stimulate motion past the sluggish part of your bowel. You might pass gas or feel some cramping—that’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great job. After the massage, you passed gas, and your G-tube output increased. That means things are moving. Your pain has improved too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I feel like a weight lifted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we wanted. We’re starting you on peripheral TPN today—total parenteral nutrition—because you’ve been NPO for three days. It’ll give you calories and nutrients through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: TPN? I’ve had that before. It’s okay, but I’d rather eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But we need to be sure your bowel is ready. We’ll try a full liquid diet tomorrow if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without nausea or vomiting. We’re going to try a full liquid diet today—broth, juice, pudding. We’ll start slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’m so happy! Can I have apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small amounts. We’ll monitor you closely. If you tolerate it, we’ll keep you on liquids and clamp your G-tube to see if it stays down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The TPN is infusing now. You’re doing well on liquids so far. No vomiting, and your belly is softer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel good. Just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal after a few days of fasting. We’re also adjusting your pain meds. We’re stopping the IV morphine and switching you to oral MS Contin 30 mg three times a day. Less IV narcotics help your bowels recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll take the pills. Can I still have liquid morphine if it flares up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 2.5 ml every four hours as needed. But we’ll watch for sedation. Your pregabalin dose is also adjusted—75 mg in the morning and at bedtime, plus one at noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full days on liquids with no vomiting. Your G-tube has been clamped, and you’re not having pain. We think you’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on full liquids for one week. Take Miralax once a day to keep your bowels moving. Continue your regular meds—misoprostol for your stomach, pilocarpine for dry eyes, and warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with MS Contin 30 mg every 12 hours for five days, then taper. Use liquid morphine for breakthrough pain. Call us if you have severe pain, fever, or can’t keep liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—see your primary doctor and Dr. ___ in one month. We’ll also check your INR and iron levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. You’ve done really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: full liquids for a week, Miralax daily, and your meds. Walk every day to keep things moving. Call if anything worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m so grateful for the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with a complex history including fibrosing mesenteritis, recurrent partial bowel obstructions, and chronic GI dysmotility, was admitted for recurrent nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Imaging confirmed a partial small bowel obstruction, managed conservatively with NPO status, G-tube to gravity, IV fluids, and pain control. G-tube output decreased from over 1200 cc/day to 500–600 cc/day. She received IV iron for iron deficiency anemia and was started on TPN on hospital day 3. Abdominal massage recommended by GI helped stimulate bowel motility, leading to passage of gas and significant pain improvement. She was transitioned to a full liquid diet on day 4, tolerated it well, and was discharged on day 5. Pain management was transitioned from IV morphine to oral MS Contin and liquid morphine for breakthrough pain. She remained ambulatory throughout and was discharged home in good condition with instructions to continue full liquids and Miralax for one week.
